content: Ocean currents are continuous, directed movements of seawater driven primarily by winds, density differences, and Earth's rotation. Surface currents, extending to about 400 meters depth, are primarily wind-driven. Global wind patterns create major gyresâlarge circular current systems in each ocean basin that flow clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern Hemisphere due to the Coriolis effect. Key surface currents like the Gulf Stream transport warm water from equatorial regions poleward, while cold-water currents like the California Current bring cooler waters toward the equator. These currents significantly influence regional climatesâareas near warm currents tend to be warmer and rainier than those at similar latitudes near cold currents. Deep ocean currents, part of the global thermohaline circulation (often called the 'ocean conveyor belt'), are driven by density differences resulting from temperature and salinity variations. Cold, salty water is denser and sinks at high latitudes, flowing along the ocean bottom toward the equator, while warmer water moves poleward near the surface. This three-dimensional circulation system connects all ocean basins and plays a critical role in global heat distribution and carbon cycling. Ocean currents also affect marine ecosystems by transporting nutrients, larvae, and plankton, creating zones of high productivity where currents bring nutrient-rich deep water to the surface (upwelling).

scenario.title: Fluid Dynamics Playground
scenario.content: Students experiment with a virtual water table representing ocean basins, manipulating factors that drive circulation patterns. The simulation allows students to adjust wind patterns, create temperature gradients, add or remove barriers (continents), and apply rotational forces (Coriolis effect). The system visualizes flow patterns using colored dyes, particles, and vector fields, showing both surface movements and three-dimensional circulation. Students can measure current speed, direction, and transport capacity while observing how these properties respond to changing conditions. Interactive tools allow creation of specialized features like underwater ridges, straits, and upwelling zones to study their effects on circulation. Challenge scenarios task students with recreating real-world current systems or designing circulation patterns that achieve specific temperature distributions. Advanced features demonstrate phenomena like El NiÃ±o/La NiÃ±a oscillations, western intensification, and how ocean circulation affects weather and climate patterns.

hypothesis.description: Students will model ocean circulation by manipulating the physical forces that drive currents. They will predict how wind patterns, density differences, and geographical features affect current formation, and explain how ocean circulation influences climate and marine ecosystems.
